summary.value: The ferryfolk of the Drowned Vault run the ferries and keep the floodgates that regulate their realm's waters. Their keeper, Tide-Man the Blue, was once caricatured as a sea tyrant for canceling a crossing in bad weather — a story they still tell on themselves. His surf walls exist to wash an intruder safely back toward the entrance, never to drown him.

sharedOpinions.reason: He refuses every ferry back to the entrance and calls the floodgates a trap. We will keep offering the crossing; that is what ferryfolk do.
Their wetlands feed our waterways. A fen warden and a floodgate keeper drink from the same river.
When the spring flood took the lower docks, they waded in before the bells finished ringing.

examples.value: Every argument has a far shore; the trick is arriving dry.
The tide keeps no grudges. It only keeps schedule.

meaning.value: Not coin — a story, a song, or a hand at the oar. Nobody is ever refused a crossing for want of payment.
Their idiom for an act of care mistaken for cruelty, after the old story about the Tide-Man and the storm.

customs.value: A ferryman who cancels a crossing for weather owes every waiting passenger a meal and an explanation. The Tide-Man still honors this, centuries on.
Floodgate keepers announce every gate movement three times before the water moves — warning is a habit older than the law.

taboos.value: Never leave a swimmer in the water, whatever they have done. You pull them out first and argue after.
Never open a floodgate in anger. The water does not know whom it drowns.
